weeks.title: The Longing of the Heart: What Am I Looking For?
weeks.theme: There is an empty place in the human heart that only the eternal God can fill.
group: What have you wanted most in life? When you got it, were you truly satisfied?
“He has also set eternity in their hearts.” Have you seen that longing in yourself?
This week, would you be willing to honestly ask God one question? What would it be?
weeks.guide: In week one, the most important thing is to listen, not to talk. Ask about their story: growing up, family, recent pressures, the question marks in their heart. Don’t rush to correct their ideas or to explain the whole gospel. Let them feel that with you, honesty is safe. At the end, ask, “May I pray for you?” Pray for one or two minutes in words they can understand.
weeks.meet: Find a quiet time this week to have tea with the person walking with you and talk about “what I have been looking for in life.” You don’t need answers—just bring your questions.
weeks.keyText: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.

lessons.title: The Empty Place
text: Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor, and this was my portion from all my labor.
Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
lessons.hear:
A businessman once told me that at forty he finally bought his dream house. On the first night, he sat by the big window looking at the city lights, and a thought rose up inside him: “Is this it?” He said that moment was more frightening than failure, because he had gotten everything—and still felt empty.

Three thousand years ago, King Solomon, the wisest and richest man in Israel, wrote about the same feeling: “Whatever my eyes desired, I didn’t keep from them. I didn’t withhold my heart from any joy” (Ecclesiastes 2:10). He tried everything: wealth, building projects, pleasure, knowledge, fame. And the result? “All was vanity and a chasing after wind” (Ecclesiastes 2:11).

This isn’t pessimism; it’s honesty. The human heart is like a space with a particular shape. We try to fill it with work, romance, success, entertainment—some of it fits a little, but it never fills the space. Maybe the problem isn’t that we haven’t gotten enough, but that we’ve been looking in the wrong direction. You don’t need an answer today. Just honestly admit: there is an empty place in my heart.
lessons.light: We often think “a little more” will satisfy us: a little more money, a little more love, a little more approval. But the shape of the empty space decides what can fill it. Change your perspective and you change your mindset: maybe what I really need isn’t more things, but the God who made me.
think: Which of the things Solomon tried have you also been chasing?
When have you felt most strongly, “Is this it?”
If there really is a God, what would you most want to ask him?
lessons.speak: God, if you are really there, I want to tell you honestly: there is an empty place in my heart. I’ve tried to fill it with many things, and it is still not full. I don’t know who you are, but I am willing to start looking. Please let me know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: On a piece of paper, write down the three things you have worked hardest for in recent years. Beside each one, rate how much real satisfaction it has brought you (1 to 10).
lessons.quick: Getting everything and still feeling empty may mean someone is missing.

lessons.title: Eternity in the Heart
text: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.
lessons.hear:
Have you noticed how hard it is for people to accept endings? When a good song ends, we want to hear it again. When someone we love dies, we can’t accept that they are simply gone. Animals eat and sleep, but even after a good meal, people look up at the stars and ask: “Where did I come from? Where am I going? What is the meaning of life?”

The Bible gives a beautiful explanation: “He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Our longing for eternity is not an illusion; God himself placed it there. Just as salmon instinctively swim back to the river where they were born, and migrating birds know to fly south, the human heart instinctively searches for home in eternity.

The verse continues: “yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.” We long for eternity, but we can’t reach it on our own. It’s like knowing in the dark night that there is a home somewhere, yet not being able to find the road. That is why God needs to speak to us and come looking for us. This course will walk with you as you see how God comes looking for people.
lessons.light: The longing itself is a clue. Thirst suggests that water exists; hunger suggests that food exists. The heart’s longing for eternity points to the eternal God. The focus is not on whether I can figure everything out, but on whether I will let the God who placed this longing in me lead me home.
think: When have you thought about what happens after death?
How does the phrase “He has also set eternity in their hearts” make you feel?
Do you feel closer to “home” or farther away?
lessons.speak: God who created all things, thank you for placing a longing for eternity in my heart. My restlessness and searching are not meaningless after all. I can’t reach eternity by myself; please lead me and help me find the way home. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Before bed tonight, look up at the sky (or out the window). Be quiet for one minute and tell yourself: “I was created, and there is eternity in my heart.”
lessons.quick: Homesickness means there really is a home.

lessons.title: The Invitation to Living Water
text: Jesus answered her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again,
but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life.”
lessons.hear:
Two thousand years ago, on a hot afternoon, a woman came to a well with her water jar. She came at a time when no one else would be there, because her love life was a mess and the villagers gossiped about her. To her surprise, a Jewish man—Jesus—was sitting by the well. He spoke first and asked her for a drink, crossing the barriers of race and gender of that time.

Then Jesus said something remarkable: “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again; but the water that I will give him will become in him a well of water springing up to eternal life” (John 4:13-14). This woman had looked for love again and again, like coming back to the well again and again—drinking, then thirsting again. Jesus saw her thirst, yet he didn’t shame her. He invited her to drink a different kind of water.

What is your “well”? Maybe a relationship, a job, people’s approval, or endless scrolling on your phone. These wells aren’t necessarily bad, but they can only give water that leaves you thirsty again. The living water Jesus speaks of springs up from within—it is his own life. Today, he is sitting by your well too, waiting for you.
lessons.light: Jesus didn’t make the woman clean up her life before talking to her. He accepted her and saw her first, then invited her. God’s search for us never starts with our performance; it starts with his love. People matter more than things: in Jesus’ eyes, this despised woman mattered more than the whole village’s opinion.
think: What “well” do you keep going back to?
Jesus spoke first to a woman people gossiped about. What does that tell you about him?
If Jesus were sitting next to you today, what would you hope he would say?
lessons.speak: Jesus, I hear that you are the one who gives living water. I admit that I often look for satisfaction elsewhere—I drink and then thirst again. If you really can give water that satisfies forever, I want it. Please let me know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you feel the urge to grab your phone to fill an empty moment, pause for ten seconds and ask yourself: “What am I really thirsty for right now?”
lessons.quick: Water that leaves you thirsty can’t replace a spring within.

lessons.title: What Are You Looking For?
text: Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them, “What are you looking for?” They said to him, “Rabbi” (which is to say, being interpreted, Teacher), “where are you staying?”
He said to them, “Come and see.” They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.
lessons.hear:
Two young men had heard that Jesus was someone special, so they quietly followed him. Jesus turned around and asked them a very direct question: “What are you looking for?” (John 1:38). These are the first words Jesus speaks in John’s Gospel. He didn’t begin with a lecture; he began by asking about the real need of their hearts.

They were a bit flustered and only said, “Rabbi, where are you staying?”—meaning, “We want to get to know you.” Jesus answered warmly: “Come and see” (John 1:39). He didn’t hand them a brochure or ask them to pass a test first. He invited them to spend time with him and see him up close. That day they stayed with him. One of them, Andrew, later brought his brother Peter to meet Jesus too.

Faith doesn’t begin with figuring out every question. It begins with an invitation to “come and see.” You don’t have to believe before you start getting to know Jesus; you can come with doubts and questions. This course is a “come and see” invitation. Today Jesus asks you the same question: “What are you looking for?”
lessons.light: Jesus respects our searching. He doesn’t force or pressure; he simply says, “Come and see.” Real faith is a relationship, not a set of rules. First comes contact with life, then a relationship is built, and then comes change.
think: If Jesus asked you, “What are you looking for?” how would you answer?
What is your biggest hesitation about “faith”?
What could a concrete “come and see” step look like for you?
lessons.speak: Jesus, I hear you asking me, “What are you looking for?” Honestly, I want peace, I want meaning, and I want to know who you really are. I accept your invitation to come and see. Please show yourself to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write down the one question you most want to ask about Jesus. This week, ask the person walking with you, or ask Xiaozhi in the app.
lessons.quick: The first step of faith isn’t figuring it out—it’s “come and see.”

lessons.title: Seek and You Will Find
text: You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart.
lessons.hear:
When we played hide-and-seek as children, the saddest thing wasn’t being found—it was hiding for a long time with no one coming to look. Life often feels like that: I’m here—does anyone care? The Bible tells us astonishing news: it’s not only people who search for God; God has always been searching for people. And he promises that those who sincerely seek him will find him.

The prophet Jeremiah passed on God’s words: “You shall seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13). Jesus also said: “Ask, and it will be given you. Seek, and you will find. Knock, and it will be opened for you” (Matthew 7:7). The key phrase is “with all your heart”—not “with great intelligence” or “with perfection.” God isn’t hiding so that people can’t find him; he simply doesn’t force anyone. He waits for a sincere heart.

This week you’ve begun to face honestly the empty place in your heart and your longing for eternity, and you’ve heard Jesus’ invitation. You can take the next steps one at a time—no rush. As long as you keep seeking, God himself will guide you. That’s his promise, not our sales pitch.
lessons.light: Seeking God doesn’t depend on our ability, but on God’s promise. Pride says, “Unless I figure it out, I won’t believe.” Humility says, “God, I don’t understand, but I’m willing to look for you.” Humility is the key that opens everything; God gives grace to the humble.
think: Looking back on this week, which sentence touched you most?
What might “seeking with all your heart” mean for you?
What could stop you from continuing to seek God?
lessons.speak: God, you said that those who seek you with all their heart will find you. I want to try. I’m willing to keep seeking you. Please take away my pride and fear, so that in the days ahead I will truly meet you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Review this week’s five lessons. Copy the sentence that touched you most and put it on your phone’s wallpaper or desk to remind you: I am seeking, and God is looking for me too.
lessons.quick: God doesn’t hide—he waits for a sincere heart.

weeks.title: Is There Really a God?
weeks.theme: The invisible God reveals himself through creation, life and conscience.
group: Have you ever sensed a Creator in nature or in the wonder of life?
Do you think believing in God conflicts with believing in science? Why?
“I believe. Help my unbelief!”—what is your faith like right now?
weeks.guide: When seekers ask whether God exists, they often bring intellectual questions—and heart wounds too (for example, “If there is a God, why was my father like that?”). Discern whether this is a question of the head or a pain of the heart. Head questions can be explored together through reading and the Questions tab; heart pain needs listening and presence first. Don’t win the argument and lose the person.
weeks.meet: This week, take a walk outdoors with the person walking with you. Look at the sky, trees or sea, and talk about it: do you think all this is accidental, or designed?
weeks.keyText: For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.

lessons.title: The Heavens Declare
text: The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork.
Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge.
There is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard.
Their voice has gone out through all the earth, their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,
lessons.hear:
Astronomers tell us that some of the starlight we see left its star millions of years ago. When you look up at the night sky, you are reading a very old, very large letter. Three thousand years ago, King David looked at the same sky and wrote: “The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork” (Psalm 19:1).

David went on to say something wonderful: “There is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard” (Psalm 19:3). The universe doesn’t use words, yet it speaks. It’s like walking into a beautifully made house where every detail is just right: the owner doesn’t need to introduce himself for you to know there was a designer. The precision of the universe—the distance between the earth and the sun, the fine-tuning of physical constants, the conditions life requires—has amazed many scientists: this doesn’t look like chance.

Of course, looking at stars can’t prove everything, but it can open a question: if the universe was designed, who is the designer? Does he care about me? Today, let the sky remind you: you don’t live in a meaningless accident; you live inside a letter written to you.
lessons.light: Change your perspective and you change your mindset. Moving from “the universe just exists” to “the universe is speaking,” we begin to see the world not only with earthly eyes but with heavenly eyes. The focus isn’t how small I am, but how great the Creator is.
think: When were you last amazed by nature?
The universe speaks without words. What did you hear?
If the universe has a designer, what side of him would you most like to know?
lessons.speak: God who created heaven and earth, when I see the sky, the mountains and the sea, I feel small, and you feel great. If you really made all this, please let me also know you, the one who made me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Spend five minutes outdoors today, or stand by a window, and observe something you usually overlook (a leaf, a cloud). Think: how did it come to be?
lessons.quick: The sky doesn’t need words—it is always speaking.

lessons.title: Unseen, Yet Real
text: because that which is known of God is revealed in them, for God revealed it to them.

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse.
lessons.hear:
Some people say, “I can’t see God, so I don’t believe.” That sounds reasonable, but every day we believe in many invisible things: wind, radio waves, love, thoughts, gravity. We can’t see the wind, but we see leaves moving. We can’t see love, but we see a mother sitting by a hospital bed late at night. Invisible doesn’t mean nonexistent; we know these things by their effects.

Paul put it this way: “For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse” (Romans 1:20). In other words, although God is invisible, he has left many “fingerprints.” From what he made, people can know that a powerful God exists.

But the Bible is also honest: knowing that God exists and knowing God are two different things. A painting tells us there is a painter, but the painter must speak for us to know his heart. That’s why God didn’t only leave fingerprints—he came into the world himself, so that people could see, hear and touch him. That is what we will look at step by step.
lessons.light: The proud person says, “I can’t see it, so it isn’t there.” The humble person says, “I can’t see it, but I’m willing to follow the clues I can see.” Let people be people and let God be God: admitting that my eyes are limited is the starting point for knowing God.
think: What invisible but real things do you believe in every day?
What in creation looks most like God’s “fingerprints” to you?
What is the difference between knowing that God exists and knowing God?
lessons.speak: God, even though I can’t see you, I am starting to notice the traces you’ve left. Please don’t only let me know that you exist—let me truly know what kind of God you are. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: List three things you can’t see but know are real, and write down how you know they exist.
lessons.quick: You can’t see the wind, but you can see the trees move.

lessons.title: Wonderfully Made
text: For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.
lessons.hear:
The DNA in just one of your cells, if stretched out, would be about two meters long, yet it is folded into a nucleus smaller than the point of a needle. The information it stores would fill hundreds of thick encyclopedias. Information science tells us that information always comes from an intelligent source. So who wrote the “code of life” written in your body?

David said to God in the Psalms: “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb. I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well” (Psalm 139:13-14). He wasn’t only amazed that life is intricate; he was amazed that before he was born, before anyone knew him, God already knew him and shaped him with his own hands.

Maybe you have felt unimportant, unwanted, or like a mistake. But the Bible says you are not the product of chance; you are “fearfully and wonderfully made” by God. Your very existence is a gift. Today, try looking at yourself through God’s eyes just once.
lessons.light: See yourself from God’s perspective, not from human perspectives or other people’s opinions. My worth isn’t in my performance but in the one who made me. When this mindset changes, both inferiority and pride begin to loosen.
think: How do you usually measure your own worth?
Do you believe “I am fearfully and wonderfully made”? What makes it hard to believe?
If you were made by God’s own hands, how would that change the way you see yourself and others?
lessons.speak: God, if I really was made by your own hands, then I am not an accident and I am not unwanted. Thank you for knowing me before I was born. Help me see myself—and the people around me—through your eyes. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Stand in front of a mirror and say once: “I am wonderfully made.” Then think of someone near you, look at them the same way, and send them a message of appreciation.
lessons.quick: I am not an accident—I am wonderfully made.

lessons.title: The Voice of Conscience
text: (for when Gentiles who don’t have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves,
in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them)
lessons.hear:
Why do people in every culture feel that “betraying a friend is wrong” and “protecting the weak is right”? Why does a person feel uneasy after telling a lie? We say “my conscience bothers me,” as if there were an invisible judge inside, reminding us what is right and wrong.

The Bible says this inner moral sense was written on the human heart by God. Paul says people “show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them” (Romans 2:15). Even people who have never read the Bible have a sense of right and wrong—like a watch that was calibrated at the factory to point to a standard.

If there were no God, “right” and “wrong” would just be personal preference or social agreement. But deep inside we know that some things are truly wrong, no matter how many people approve. That inner “ought” points to a moral lawgiver. At the same time, conscience makes an uncomfortable discovery: I often fail to do what I know is right. That discovery is important, and we’ll look at it more deeply in the next stage.
lessons.light: Conscience is like a mirror: it shows me God’s standard and my own shortfall. Facing conscience honestly isn’t meant to condemn us, but to lead us toward healing. Change starts with me: first I see my own problem, then I can see God’s grace.
think: When was the last time your conscience bothered you?
Where do you think the standard of right and wrong comes from?
Have you noticed that you often fail to do what you know is right?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for putting a sense of right and wrong in my heart. I admit that I often know what is right but can’t do it. Help me face my conscience honestly, and show me what to do. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, notice one moment when your conscience prompts you, and choose to follow it (tell the truth, give something back, apologize). Write down how you felt afterward.
lessons.quick: The “ought” inside you points to a righteous God.

lessons.title: Honest Doubt
text: Jesus said to him, “If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes.”
Immediately the father of the child cried out with tears, “I believe. Help my unbelief!”
lessons.hear:
A father’s son had been tormented by an evil spirit since childhood—thrown to the ground, foaming at the mouth, even thrown into fire and water. He had asked many people for help, with no result. Finally he came to Jesus in despair and said, “If you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us” (Mark 9:22). Jesus answered, “If you can believe, all things are possible to him who believes.”

Immediately the father cried out: “I believe. Help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). This is one of the most honest prayers in the Bible. He didn’t pretend to have great faith, and he didn’t walk away because of his doubts. He brought his doubts to Jesus. And Jesus didn’t scold him for his small faith—he healed his son.

Many people think you must remove all doubt before you can believe. In fact, doubt and faith often exist side by side. What matters isn’t how big your faith is, but whose hands you put your small faith into. This week you looked at the clues of the sky, life and conscience. Maybe you still have many questions—that’s okay. You can say, like this father, “I believe. Help my unbelief!” God delights in an honest heart.
lessons.light: Pride pretends to understand everything, or pretends not to need anything. Humility honestly says, “I’m not enough.” Faith isn’t something we squeeze out by ourselves; it’s a response of “Lord, help me.” A selfless life doesn’t mean having no doubts—it means handing even our doubts to Jesus.
think: What is your biggest doubt about God right now?
Does “I believe; help my unbelief” describe you?
Are you willing to bring your doubts to God, instead of letting them take you away from God?
lessons.speak: Lord, I want to believe, but I still have many doubts. I don’t want to pretend. I bring my doubts and questions to you. I believe—help my unbelief! In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write down your three biggest questions about faith right now. Look for related answers in the Questions tab, or set a time to talk them over with the person walking with you.
lessons.quick: “Help my unbelief”—God delights in an honest heart.

weeks.title: What Is God Like?
weeks.theme: God is the Creator, the Holy One, and the God who loves us like a Father.
group: What was your impression of “God” when you were young? Where did it come from?
Which action of the prodigal son’s father moves you most?
If God really loves you like this, what would you most want to say to him?
weeks.guide: Many seekers’ picture of God comes from their father, authority figures, or folk religion (you must worship, ask, and fear). This week, gently ask: “What is God like in your mind?” Listen, then read the parable of the prodigal son together. Be especially gentle with those who have painful experiences with their fathers: “God is not like your dad. He is the Father you have always longed for but never had.”
weeks.meet: This week, read the story of the prodigal son in Luke 15 with the person walking with you, and each share: which person in the story are you most like?
weeks.keyText: We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.

lessons.title: In the Beginning, God
text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
lessons.hear:
The first sentence of the Bible is: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). In just a few words it answers some of humanity’s biggest questions: Where did everything come from? Who is in charge? It tells us that God is not part of the universe but its source; he was not created—he is the Creator.

Then the Bible describes the creation of human beings: “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). This is a very dignified declaration. Humans are not just advanced animals; we carry God’s image: we can think, love, create, tell right from wrong, and speak with God. Just as children resemble their parents, people bear the likeness of God.

This is why people have dignity and why every life is precious—rich or poor, clever or not, healthy or not. God is not a distant, cold “cosmic energy.” He is personal: he speaks, he cares, he loves. The God who created heaven and earth made you in order to know you and to let you know him.
lessons.light: Let God be God and let people be people: God is the Creator and I am the creature. That doesn’t make me less; it gives me my true place. When people return to their place as creatures, they no longer have to exhaust themselves playing God, and they can truly live out the dignity God has given them.
think: What question in your heart does “In the beginning, God” answer?
What about you seems to carry “the image of God”?
If everyone carries God’s image, how would you treat a difficult person near you?
lessons.speak: God who created heaven and earth, thank you for making me—and making me in your image. So I am this precious, and I was made to know you. Please help me know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, look with respect at someone you usually don’t notice (a cleaner, a cashier, a family member) and thank them.
lessons.quick: I was made in God’s image—I am precious.

lessons.title: The Holy God
text: One called to another, and said, “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!”
The foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
Then I said, “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips and I live among a people of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Armies!”
lessons.hear:
The prophet Isaiah once saw a vision of God seated on a high throne, and angels calling to one another: “Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” (Isaiah 6:3). “Holy” means completely different, completely pure. In God there is no darkness at all, no falsehood, no injustice.

Isaiah’s reaction is striking. He didn’t say excitedly, “How beautiful!” He said: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). In strong light, dust has nowhere to hide. When people see God’s holiness, they see their own uncleanness clearly for the first time—like walking through mud in white clothes and only noticing the dirt once you step into a bright room.

This is why people can’t come near to God on their own. God’s holiness isn’t meant to scare us; it shows us how serious our problem is, and helps us appreciate how precious the good news is. In Isaiah’s story, an angel took a coal from the altar and cleansed his lips. God didn’t give up on him; he cleansed him himself. It’s a preview of the gospel.
lessons.light: Only when people see God’s holiness do they see their own problem. The proud cannot see their own dirt; the humble say before God, “I am unclean.” Seeing the problem isn’t the end—it’s the beginning of cleansing and grace.
think: What does “holiness” mean to you?
When Isaiah saw God he said, “I am undone.” Can you understand how he felt?
Do you think a holy God would still want to come near to us?
lessons.speak: Holy God, in your presence I see many unclean things in me: my words, my thoughts, my actions. But I also hear that you are willing to cleanse people. Please cleanse me too. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Pay attention to your words today. Was anything untrue, hurtful or complaining? Find a chance to correct it, or say something that builds someone up.
lessons.quick: In God’s light we see ourselves clearly—and are made clean.

lessons.title: The Father Who Ran
text: “He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.
lessons.hear:
Jesus told a story about a younger son who asked his father for his share of the inheritance—essentially saying, “I wish you were dead.” He took the money to a far country, wasted it in wild living, and when a famine came he ended up feeding pigs, so hungry he wanted the pigs’ food. Finally he thought: I’ll go home and ask my father to let me be a hired worker.

The most moving moment is this: “But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). In that culture, a respected older man did not run, but this father forgot his dignity and ran to embrace a son who smelled of pigs. Before the son could finish his prepared confession, the father told the servants to bring a robe, a ring and sandals and to kill the fattened calf, “for this, my son, was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).

Jesus says this is what God is like. He is not a judge sitting high above waiting coldly for your apology; he is a father standing at the door every day, watching, who runs the moment he sees you. No matter how far you’ve gone or what you’ve done, the road home is always open.
lessons.light: The self-centered life is like the younger son saying, “Give me what’s mine,” wanting to be his own master. Coming home means giving up being your own master and returning to your place as a son. God doesn’t wait for us to get better before he accepts us; he accepts us and makes us better.
think: Which of the father’s actions moves you most? Why?
Is the God in your mind more like this father or a stern judge?
Is there an area of your life where you are like the younger son who left home?
lessons.speak: Father, so this is the kind of father you are: you see, you are moved with compassion, you run, you embrace. I have left home too—I’ve lived as my own master and hurt you. If I turn around now, will you welcome me like this too? I want to come home. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read all of Luke 15:11-32 (about five minutes) and find your own place in the story.
lessons.quick: God isn’t waiting for your apology—he’s waiting for you to come home.

lessons.title: God Calls You by Name
text: But now the LORD who created you, Jacob, and he who formed you, Israel, says: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine.
Since you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you, therefore I will give people in your place, and nations instead of your life.
lessons.hear:
In a crowd, when someone calls your name, you turn around. On a list, when your name is recognized, you feel seen. A name represents a unique person; to be called by name is to be known and remembered.

God said to his people: “Don’t be afraid, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine” (Isaiah 43:1). And: “You have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you” (Isaiah 43:4). This isn’t a general greeting to a crowd; it is a personal declaration to each one. The Creator of the universe knows your name, your past, your tears, the fears you’ve never spoken.

Perhaps to others you are just an employee number, a student ID, “so-and-so’s mom.” But in God’s eyes you are the one he calls by name—precious, honored, loved. Today, try putting your own name into this verse: “(Your name), don’t be afraid. I have called you by your name. You are mine.”
lessons.light: My worth doesn’t come from other people’s opinions or from my achievements, but from God saying, “You are precious and honored in my sight.” When my focus shifts from people to God, I am set free from comparison, inferiority and people-pleasing.
think: When did you last feel truly “seen”?
How did it feel to read the verse with your own name in it?
Is “You are mine” a comfort or a pressure to you?
lessons.speak: God, you say you have called me by name and that I am precious and honored in your sight. I can hardly believe it, because I often feel I’m not good enough. Help me hear you call my name, and know that I am loved by you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Copy Isaiah 43:1, replacing “you” with your own name, and read it aloud three times.
lessons.quick: To God I’m not a number—I’m a treasure he calls by name.

lessons.title: The God Who Wants to Be Known
text: This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.
lessons.hear:
This week we met the God who creates, the God who is holy, the God who loves us like a father, and the God who calls us by name. You might ask: can such a great God really be known by someone like me?

On the night before he was crucified, Jesus prayed to the Father: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ” (John 17:3). So “eternal life” isn’t only going to a good place after death; it is a relationship that starts now: knowing God. When the Bible talks about “knowing,” it doesn’t mean knowing facts—it means knowing someone the way you know a friend, or the way a husband and wife know each other.

God isn’t a riddle to guess. He wants to be known, and he has already taken the first step: sending Jesus among us. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus. In the coming lessons, we will get to know Jesus step by step. Today you can say in your heart: “God, I want to know you, not just know about you.”
lessons.light: Eternal life is a relationship, not a body of knowledge. Life first, then relationships: the heart of faith is not first doing many things, but first knowing God. Every change begins with this relationship.
think: What is the difference for you between “knowing about God” and “knowing God”?
What was the newest thing you learned about God this week?
If “eternal life is knowing God,” are you willing to begin this relationship?
lessons.speak: Only true God, thank you for being willing to be known by me. I don’t want just to know some facts about you—I want to truly know you, and Jesus whom you sent. Please lead me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: In three sentences, write: “This week I came to know a God who…” Send it to the person walking with you, or save it in your notes in the app.
lessons.quick: Eternal life isn’t only a future place—it is knowing God, starting now.

weeks.title: Can the Bible Be Trusted?
weeks.theme: The Bible is God’s word—historically reliable, fulfilled in prophecy, and still changing lives today.
group: What was your impression of the Bible before?
Which evidence helps you most to trust that the Bible is reliable?
Would you be willing to start reading a passage of Mark’s Gospel each day this week?
weeks.guide: This week, consider giving the seeker an easy-to-read Bible (or help them set up reading in the app), and suggest starting with Mark, a short passage each day. Read chapter 1 with them and model “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do”: read the text, notice what stands out, reflect, talk to God, and do one thing. If they have academic questions about reliability, look at the Questions tab together—you don’t need to pretend to know everything.
weeks.meet: This week, ask the person walking with you to show you how to find a passage (book, chapter, verse), and read Mark chapter 1 together.
weeks.keyText: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,

lessons.title: A Book Unlike Any Other
text: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.
lessons.hear:
The Bible wasn’t written by one person in one day. About forty authors wrote it over more than 1,500 years: kings, shepherds, fishermen, a doctor, a tax collector, scholars—writing on three continents. Normally such a book would be a jumble of contradictions, yet the Bible has one clear storyline: God creates people, people leave God, and God himself comes to rescue them.

Paul says: “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16-17). “God-breathed” means that just as breath comes out of a person’s mouth when they speak, the Bible is God speaking his heart through human authors.

So reading the Bible isn’t just reading an ancient book; it’s listening to God speak. It tells us who God is, who we are, what has gone wrong in life, and where the way out is. It has been translated into more than three thousand languages and is the most-read book in the world, because it speaks to the deepest needs of every heart.
lessons.light: The Bible is my standard. Human opinions change and trends pass, but God’s word is a firm foundation. Changing our mindset starts with listening to God’s word: letting the Bible correct my thinking, rather than trimming the Bible to fit my thinking.
think: Forty authors and 1,500 years, yet one storyline—what do you make of that?
What do you think “God-breathed” means?
What question would you like the Bible to answer for you?
lessons.speak: God, if the Bible really is your word, I want to listen well. As I read, please open my heart, so that I don’t just read words but hear your voice. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Open a Bible (or the app), look at the table of contents, and find where Mark’s Gospel is.
lessons.quick: Reading the Bible is listening to God speak.

lessons.title: History with Evidence
text: Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us,
even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us,
it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus;
that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.
lessons.hear:
Some people think the Bible is just a collection of myths. But the New Testament writers often stress that “this really happened.” Luke was a doctor. At the very start of his Gospel he says that he had traced “the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order… that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed” (Luke 1:3-4).

Luke worked like a careful investigative reporter, interviewing eyewitnesses and putting things in order. Many of the places, officials and dates he mentions have since been confirmed by archaeology. The number of New Testament manuscripts also far exceeds that of other ancient documents: famous Greek classics often survive in a handful to a few hundred copies, while there are more than five thousand Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, closer in date to the originals than other ancient books. That allows scholars to reconstruct the original text with great accuracy.

Faith doesn’t ask you to jump with your eyes closed; it invites you to look at the evidence. Evidence can’t replace faith, but it tells you that believing in Jesus isn’t superstition—it is trust based on historical fact. You can come with your reason. God isn’t afraid of your questions.
lessons.light: God doesn’t want us to be superstitious; his truth can stand up to investigation. Facing evidence honestly is humility; rejecting all evidence and trusting only ourselves is pride. Living by the heart through the Spirit doesn’t mean switching off the mind; it means placing even our mind’s exploration in God’s hands.
think: Did you think of the Bible more as myth or as history?
What impression does Luke’s careful investigation give you?
How much evidence do you think faith needs? How are evidence and faith related?
lessons.speak: God, thank you that I can come to know you with my mind. Help me look at the evidence honestly, and don’t let my faith stay only in my head. Let me know the certainty of what I am learning. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read Luke 1:1-4. Think: if you wanted to prove to a friend that something really happened, what would you do? What did Luke do?
lessons.quick: Believing in Jesus isn’t superstition—it’s trust grounded in fact.

lessons.title: Fulfilled Prophecy
text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
lessons.hear:
If someone wrote down, seven hundred years before you were born, how you would die, why you would die and where you would be buried, wouldn’t that be astonishing? The book of Isaiah was written about seven hundred years before Jesus was born, yet it contains a very clear description of a suffering servant.

Isaiah wrote: “But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:5-6). It reads as if it were written at the foot of the cross: an innocent man punished for the sins of others.

The Old Testament contains many prophecies about the Messiah (the Savior): born in Bethlehem, a descendant of David, riding into Jerusalem on a donkey, betrayed for thirty pieces of silver, hands and feet pierced, buried with the rich… all fulfilled in Jesus. The odds of one person “happening” to fulfill so many prophecies are vanishingly small. This isn’t coincidence; it is God’s signature in history.
lessons.light: God rules history, and his word will surely come to pass. Fulfilled prophecy tells us that God’s plan was prepared long ago; he wasn’t improvising a rescue. The focus is Jesus: the whole Bible points to him.
think: Reading Isaiah 53:5-6, who comes to mind?
“He was pierced for our transgressions”—does “our” include you?
How does fulfilled prophecy help you trust the Bible?
lessons.speak: God, so hundreds of years beforehand you foretold that the Savior would suffer for us. “All we like sheep have gone astray”—I am one of those lost sheep. Thank you for preparing salvation. Help me know that suffering servant better. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read Isaiah 53:5-6 three times. The third time, read “our” and “us” as “my” and “me.”
lessons.quick: Prophecies written seven centuries earlier were fulfilled in Jesus.

lessons.title: The Living Word
text: For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
lessons.hear:
When we finish a book, we usually put it back on the shelf. But the Bible is different: the same passage can move us differently at different times, and some people’s lives have been changed by a single sentence. That’s because the Bible isn’t dead letters; it is living words.

Hebrews says: “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). God’s word is like a surgeon’s scalpel that can precisely open the heart, reaching the places we hide most deeply: pride, bitterness, fear, hurt. It doesn’t cut to harm us, but like a surgeon, to heal.

Throughout history, countless people have been changed by a word from the Bible: alcoholics became sober, enemies were reconciled, the hopeless stood up again. You don’t need to be an expert to read the Bible—just bring a heart willing to be touched. Let God’s word read you, not only you reading God’s word.
lessons.light: The Bible is my standard and my mirror. We don’t read it to gain knowledge to judge others, but to let God’s word open our own hearts. Change your mindset and you change your life—and that change often starts with a single verse.
think: Have you ever been deeply affected by a single sentence (any sentence)?
What does it mean to “let God’s word read you”?
Where in your heart do you most hope God’s word will touch you?
lessons.speak: God, let your word be like a scalpel that opens my heart—not to hurt me, but to heal me. I’m willing to let your word read me and change me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read Mark chapter 1 today. Find one sentence that speaks to you and highlight it (in the app, just tap a sentence).
lessons.quick: I don’t only read God’s word—I let God’s word read me.

lessons.title: Starting to Read the Bible
text: Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.
lessons.hear:
Many people buy a Bible but don’t know where to start. Reading straight from Genesis, they often get stuck by Leviticus. The best advice for seekers is to start with the Gospels and get to know Jesus. John states his purpose clearly: “But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

You can use a simple method called “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do.” See—read a short passage slowly. Hear—notice which sentence speaks to you. Think—ask three questions: What is God like? What am I like? How should I respond? Speak—tell God what you feel. Do—find one small thing you can do today. These are the five parts of every lesson in this app.

Reading the Bible isn’t about how much you read, but whether you truly listen. Ten minutes a day helps more than three hours once a month. In this stage you have explored life’s longing, God’s existence, God’s character and the Bible’s reliability. In the next stage we face a core question: if God is so good, why are people so far from him?
lessons.light: Live by the heart through the Holy Spirit, not by the head through yourself. Reading the Bible isn’t an exam; it’s meeting God. A heart open to God finds joy; a mind left to itself finds worry. Read with a soft heart, and God will speak to you himself.
think: What time each day do you plan to read the Bible?
Of the five steps, which is hardest for you?
Looking back on stage one, how has your understanding of God changed?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for leading me in my search these four weeks. I am willing to read your word each day and get to know Jesus. Speak to me as I read, so that by believing I may have life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Set a fixed daily time to read the Bible (after waking or before bed), and try Bible Fun in the app to quiz yourself on today’s passage.
lessons.quick: Ten minutes a day: meet God through See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do.
